posts.title: Edge vs Cloud Video Analytics: Where Should AI Inference Run?
posts.seoTitle: Edge vs Cloud Video Analytics: Where AI Runs
posts.excerpt: Edge vs cloud video analytics compared: bandwidth, alert latency, privacy, WAN outages and cost structure, plus when a hybrid model makes sense.
posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: Remote monitoring setup with an on-site video console, a laptop and a phone connected to multiple sites through secure access
takeaways: Edge video analytics runs AI models on hardware at the site; cloud video analytics sends video or frames to a provider's data center for analysis.
Edge suits sites with many cameras, limited upload bandwidth, strict data policies or unreliable internet links.
Cloud suits small, well-connected sites that cannot host or maintain compute hardware.
Most multi-site organizations land on a hybrid: inference at each site, with alerts, health and configuration managed centrally.

sections.text: **Short answer:** Run AI inference at the edge, on hardware at the site, when you have many cameras, limited or costly upload bandwidth, a policy that video must stay on site, or alerts that must keep working during internet outages. Cloud inference makes sense for small, well-connected sites that cannot host any compute hardware. Many multi-site organizations combine the two: inference on site, management and oversight in the cloud.

Where AI inference runs sounds like an infrastructure detail, but it shapes most of a video analytics deployment: how much bandwidth each site needs, how quickly alerts arrive, who holds the video, what happens when the internet drops and how costs grow as you add cameras. This guide walks through each factor in plain terms.
What is the difference between edge and cloud video analytics?

The difference is where the AI model looks at the video. With edge video analytics, the model runs on a server, appliance or camera at the site. With cloud video analytics, video, clips or frames travel over the internet to a provider's data center, where the model runs.

In both cases the cameras can be the same. What changes is the path video takes before it is analyzed, and with it the network, privacy and resilience profile of the whole system. Our glossary entry on [edge AI video analytics](/glossary/edge-ai-video-analytics) covers the term in more depth, and cloud-hosted surveillance more broadly is often called [VSaaS (video surveillance as a service)](/glossary/vsaas).
How do edge and cloud analytics compare?
The table below summarizes the trade-offs. Neither column is right for every site; the point is to see which constraints matter most for yours.

rows: On a server or appliance at the site, often GPU-accelerated
Low; only events and metadata need to leave the site
High; video or frames must be uploaded for analysis
Local; no internet round trip before detection
Depends on upload speed and the round trip to the provider
Video stays inside the site network
Video leaves the site and is processed by the provider

Minimal; cameras and possibly a gateway

sections.text: For a side-by-side view with guidance on when to choose each, see our [on-prem vs cloud video analytics comparison](/compare/on-prem-vs-cloud-video-analytics).
Why does bandwidth matter so much?

Video is heavy, and AI needs a steady supply of it. A detection model watching for intrusion or PPE compliance has to see frames continuously, not only when someone remembers to look. For cloud inference, that means a constant upload from every analyzed camera, at a quality high enough for the model to work.

Many sites have far more download than upload capacity, and their links are shared with billing, ERP, voice and other business traffic. Adding a continuous stream from each camera can saturate the link, or force resolution and frame rate down to a level that hurts detection. Edge analytics avoids the problem: video travels only across the local network to the on-site node, and what leaves the site is a small stream of alerts, snapshots and metadata.
How does latency affect alerts?

For some use cases a short delay does not matter. For others, such as a person entering a restricted zone near moving machinery or someone climbing a perimeter fence at night, the value of an alert drops with every second.

Edge inference takes the internet out of the detection path. Frames are analyzed on the local network and the alert is raised on site, so latency depends mainly on the model and the capacity of the node. With cloud inference, every detection also depends on upload speed, network congestion and the provider's processing queue. Both can be fast in good conditions; the difference shows when conditions are not good.
What about privacy and data residency?

This is often the deciding factor. With edge analytics, video stays inside the site network, and only the information needed to act on an event leaves it. With cloud analytics, video leaves the site and is processed by the provider, which raises questions your security, legal and compliance teams will want answered:

items: Where, physically, is video stored and processed, and in which country?
Who at the provider can access it, and is that access logged?
How long is video retained, and how is it deleted?
Is customer video used to train or improve the provider's models?

sections.text: None of these questions rules the cloud out, but each needs a clear, written answer. If your policy is simply that video must not leave the premises, edge inference is the straightforward way to meet it.
What happens when the internet goes down?

WAN links fail, get congested or are cut during maintenance, and remote sites such as warehouses, plants, branches and towers often have the least reliable connectivity. With cloud inference, an outage means analysis stops or degrades until the link returns. With edge inference, detection and local alerting carry on, and events can be synchronized to the central system once the connection is back.
Ask any vendor exactly what keeps working during a WAN outage: recording, detection, local alerts, and how events are reconciled afterward.
How do the costs compare?
Without quoting numbers, the two models differ in the shape of their costs rather than simply in size.

items: **Edge** has an upfront hardware component, because each site needs a node with enough compute, usually GPU capacity, for its cameras and detections. Software, support and maintenance sit on top. Adding many cameras at a site may mean adding node capacity.
**Cloud** has little upfront hardware but ongoing subscription fees that usually scale per camera or per stream, plus the cost of the upload bandwidth the analytics consume.

sections.text: The comparison that matters is total cost over the life of the deployment, including bandwidth upgrades, hardware refresh, support and the operational cost of missed or late alerts. With many cameras per site, edge tends to be easier to scale; with a handful of cameras at a well-connected site, cloud can be simpler.
When does a hybrid model make sense?
For most multi-site organizations, the realistic answer is not edge or cloud but both, each doing the job it suits.

In a hybrid model, inference and recording run at each site, close to the cameras, while a central cloud layer handles what benefits from being central: one view of every site, alert review, camera health, configuration, user management and reporting. Video stays where it is captured; metadata moves.

This pattern keeps the bandwidth, latency, privacy and resilience benefits of the edge, while giving head office or a regional control room the oversight that cloud systems are known for. When evaluating a hybrid platform, check that both layers behave as one system, so that a configuration change, an alert and a health issue all refer to the same camera.
Where does OrionAlerts fit?

OrionAlerts runs [AI video analytics](/solutions/ai-analytics) at the edge. In the standard deployment, an on-site [Nebula OS](/nebula-os) node runs video, recording and AI inference inside your network. GPU acceleration is used where AI analytics are enabled, and the node is sized to the channel count and the detections running. Cameras connect through ONVIF, RTSP and vendor SDKs, so the cameras you already own can be used.

For multi-site estates, each site runs its own node, and Orion Cloud provides the central management layer. It synchronizes health, alerts, configuration and operational metadata, so teams get one view across every location without uploading raw video. Partners can also deploy and manage nodes on behalf of their clients. Alerts reach operators through the dashboard, mobile app and email. Because recording and detection run on site, they do not depend on a fast internet link, and the on-site deployment is built to work through constrained or intermittent WAN links.
FAQs
Is edge video analytics more secure than cloud analytics?

Not automatically, but it removes a major exposure. Edge analytics keeps video inside the site network, so footage is not sent over the internet or held by an outside provider. Overall security still depends on how the on-site systems and any central management layer are configured, patched, access-controlled and monitored.
Can I use edge analytics with my existing cameras?

Usually, yes. Most edge platforms discover and configure IP cameras through ONVIF and pull their video over RTSP, and some also use vendor SDKs. Compatibility should still be confirmed model by model, including older cameras and recorders. Our guide to [adding AI to existing CCTV cameras](/blogs/add-ai-to-existing-cctv-cameras) covers the checks.
Does edge video analytics need a GPU?

Usually, yes. Running detection models continuously on many camera streams relies on hardware acceleration, typically a GPU in the on-site server or appliance. The right size depends on how many cameras are analyzed, their resolution and frame rate, and which detections run on each, so ask vendors to size the node for your sites.
Can edge analytics still be managed centrally?

Yes. In a hybrid design, each site runs inference locally, while a central layer collects alerts, health status and configuration from every site. Head office or a regional control room gets one view of the whole estate, and settings can be managed centrally, without moving raw video off site.

posts.title: Surveillance Asset Management: Building a Live Camera and NVR Register Across Sites
posts.excerpt: Build a live register of cameras, NVRs and network devices across sites: what to record, custody, warranty, lifecycle and keeping it in sync.
posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: Surveillance asset lifecycle around an asset register screen: procurement, registration with serial number, deployment and assignment, operation and monitoring, maintenance and service, upgrade and end-of-life disposal
takeaways: A surveillance asset register is one record of every camera, recorder, server and network device, with its location, owner, warranty, contract and service history.
Spreadsheet registers drift because the estate changes faster than anyone updates them, and nothing checks the list against the devices on the network.
Connect the register to live device data so offline, replaced or moved devices show up as changes, not surprises at audit time.
Link each asset to its warranty and AMC so a failure can be raised against the right vendor and contract.

sections.text: **Short answer:** Surveillance asset management means keeping one live register of every camera, NVR, server, switch and storage device across your sites, with each asset's identity, location, owner, warranty, maintenance contract and history. The register stays accurate only when it is connected to the devices themselves, so that status changes, replacements and moves show up automatically.

Ask a multi-site organization how many cameras it has, and the answer often depends on who you ask. Procurement has purchase orders, the installer has a handover sheet, the AMC vendor has its own list and the security team has whatever the NVRs show. A proper register brings these sources together and keeps them true.
What is a surveillance asset register?

It is the single, authoritative list of the physical devices that make up your video estate, together with the facts needed to operate, maintain and replace them. It covers more than cameras: NVRs and DVRs, servers, storage, network switches, PoE injectors, encoders, UPS units and monitors all affect whether video is captured and available.

A good register answers everyday questions quickly. Which cameras are at this branch? Who is responsible for them? Is this NVR still under warranty? When was this camera last serviced, and how often has it failed?
What should you record for each asset?
Use a consistent set of fields for every device type. The exact list will vary, but these cover most needs:

rows: A stable reference that survives replacements and moves
Drives compatibility, spares and firmware decisions
Ties the record to one physical unit for warranty and audits
Lets a technician find it and an investigator know what it covers
Links a camera to where its video is stored
Names who is accountable, centrally and at the site
Shows whether a fault is a claim or a paid repair
Shows who must respond, and under which terms
In store, installed, in repair, retired or disposed
Every fault, visit, replaced part and outcome

sections.text: Keep the list short enough that people will actually fill it in.
Who is accountable for each camera?

Custody is the part spreadsheets most often get wrong. A register should name two parties for each asset: the owner, usually a site or department accountable for the device, and the custodian, the person or team who looks after it day to day.

Custody changes when staff move, sites are reorganized or a device is sent for repair. Record each change with a date and a reason. When a device leaves a site for repair or replacement, the register should show where it went, who has it and when it is due back, so that a missing camera is never simply missing.
How should warranty and AMC be tracked?

Every asset should point to its warranty terms and, where relevant, its [annual maintenance contract (AMC)](/glossary/amc-annual-maintenance-contract). That link is what turns a fault into an action. If a camera fails under warranty, the claim goes to the supplier; if it is covered by an AMC, a service request goes to the contracted vendor under the agreed terms.

Track warranty and contract end dates in one place, and set reminders well ahead of expiry so renewals are a decision rather than a lapse. Our [CCTV AMC management checklist](/blogs/cctv-amc-management-checklist) covers contract terms, preventive maintenance and vendor scorecards in more detail.
How do you manage the asset lifecycle?

Each device moves through a lifecycle: procurement, registration, deployment, operation and maintenance, upgrade or replacement, and finally retirement and disposal. Recording each stage gives you a history you can plan with.

items: **Procurement and registration.** Create the record when the device arrives, not when someone gets around to it, and capture the serial number at that point.
**Deployment.** Record the site, position, recorder channel and custodian when the device is installed.
**Operation and maintenance.** Log every fault, visit and part replacement against the asset.
**Replacement.** When a camera is swapped, retire the old record and link the new one to the same position, so the history is kept.
**Retirement and disposal.** Record how and when the device left the estate, including how any stored footage or data was handled.

sections.text: Over time, lifecycle data shows which models fail most often and which devices are nearing end of life, which makes refresh budgets easier to plan.
Why do spreadsheet registers drift?
Spreadsheets work for a while, then drift for predictable reasons:

items: **The estate changes faster than the file.** Cameras are added, moved and replaced during routine work, and nobody updates the sheet afterward.
**There are several copies.** Each site, vendor and team keeps its own version, and the versions disagree.
**Nothing checks the list against reality.** A spreadsheet cannot tell you that a camera it lists has been offline for a week, or was replaced by a different model.
**History is lost.** Overwriting a cell erases what was there, so the custody and service trail disappears.
**Ownership is unclear.** When everyone can edit the file, nobody is responsible for it being right.

sections.text: The result is a register that is accurate on the day of an audit and wrong soon after.
How do you keep the register in sync with live devices?

Stop relying on people to notice changes, and let the devices report them. When the register is connected to the system that already talks to your cameras and recorders, it can reflect status, identity and firmware directly.
In practice, that means:

items: **Reconcile the register against the devices actually found** on the network and recorders, so unknown or missing devices stand out.

**Link health status to each asset**, so an offline camera or a recorder that has stopped recording appears on the asset record. See how [camera health monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring) works.
**Treat replacements as events**, so a new serial number at a known position updates the record and keeps its history.
**Raise service requests from the asset**, so maintenance is tied to the right contract and vendor.
**Review exceptions on a schedule**, such as devices with no owner, an expired warranty or no recent health data.

sections.text: What should your register checklist cover?
Use this checklist to judge whether your register is ready to run a multi-site estate.

rows: Every camera, recorder, server, switch and storage device in the video path is listed
Each record has a serial number, model and stable asset ID
Site, building and position are recorded for every device
Each asset has a named owner and custodian, with a change log
Warranty and AMC are linked to each asset, with expiry reminders
Health and recording status appear on the asset record
Stage and service history are kept, not overwritten
One register shared by security, facilities, IT and vendors

sections.text: How does OrionAlerts handle surveillance asset management?

OrionAlerts includes [Asset Tracking](/solutions/asset-tracking) and [AMC Management](/solutions/amc-management) as modules of one platform, alongside the VMS, AI video analytics and camera health monitoring, all running on [Nebula OS](/nebula-os). Asset Tracking keeps one register of cameras, recorders, servers and network devices with location, custodian, serial number, warranty and documents. Teams find any asset by serial number, QR code or barcode, every transfer is logged, and the custody history can be exported for audits. AMC Management tracks maintenance contracts, warranties, preventive maintenance, service requests, vendor performance and SLAs.

Every device connected to the platform through ONVIF, RTSP or vendor SDKs is also an asset record, so the register stays in step with the live estate instead of drifting like a spreadsheet. Because the modules share that record, an alert, an outage and a service ticket all point to the same device, and a failing camera can raise a service request against the right vendor and contract. For multi-site organizations, Orion Cloud gives one central view of alerts, camera health, assets and maintenance across every location.
FAQs
What is the difference between asset tracking and camera health monitoring?

Asset tracking records what each device is, where it is, who owns it and its warranty and service history. Health monitoring checks whether the device is working right now. They are most useful when they share one record, so a fault appears on the asset it affects.
Should NVRs and network switches be in the same register as cameras?

Yes. A camera is only useful if its recorder, switch, storage and power are working, so the register should cover every device in the video path and show how they connect. Recording which recorder channel and switch a camera depends on also speeds up fault-finding, because a technician can see at once what else an outage affects.
How often should a surveillance asset register be audited?

Set a regular cycle that suits your estate, and audit after major changes such as site openings, refits or vendor handovers. A register linked to live device data needs fewer manual audits, because missing and changed devices surface on their own.
Can an existing spreadsheet be turned into a live register?

Usually, yes. Clean it first: remove duplicates, agree on the field list and fill gaps such as serial numbers and locations. Then import it and reconcile it against the devices actually connected at each site, so devices with no record, and records with no device, stand out from the start.

posts.title: AI Video Analytics Buyer's Guide: How to Evaluate Vendors
posts.seoTitle: How to Evaluate AI Video Analytics Vendors
posts.excerpt: How to evaluate AI video analytics vendors: existing-camera support, edge or cloud inference, data residency, multi-site control, pilots and support.
posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: AI video analytics alert console showing intrusion, fall, fire and smoke, missing PPE and camera tamper detections from site cameras, with the same alerts arriving on a mobile phone
takeaways: Start from your problems and your cameras, not a vendor's feature list: define the events you need detected and the sites where they matter.
Confirm compatibility with your existing cameras and recorders, and ask exactly where inference runs and where video is stored.
Run a pilot on your own cameras and sites, with success criteria agreed in writing before it starts.
Weigh multi-site management, camera health, integration and local support as heavily as the list of detections.

sections.text: **Short answer:** Evaluate AI video analytics vendors on fit with your estate and your problems, not on demo videos. Check that they work with the cameras and recorders you already own, where AI inference runs and where video is stored, how they manage many sites, whether they monitor camera health, how they integrate with your systems and what support looks like near your sites. Then prove it with a pilot on your own cameras, judged against criteria agreed in advance.

Buying AI video analytics is harder than buying cameras. Every vendor has a polished demo and the feature lists look alike, but what matters is how the system behaves on your cameras, network and sites. This guide sets out the questions to ask and a checklist for comparing vendors side by side. It is written with Indian multi-site organizations in mind, where mixed camera brands, branch networks with uneven connectivity and partner-led installation are common, but the approach applies anywhere.
What should you define before talking to vendors?
Write down what you want the system to do, in operational terms. A short brief makes every vendor answer the same question.

items: **The events that matter.** For example, perimeter intrusion at night, PPE compliance on a production floor or vehicles in a restricted area. Browse common [AI video analytics use cases](/use-cases) for ideas.
**Where they matter.** Which sites, which cameras and which hours.
**Who acts on an alert.** A central control room, site security or a shift supervisor, and how each needs to be reached.
**Your estate.** Camera and recorder brands and models, the number of sites and the connectivity at each.
**Your constraints.** Data policies, IT security requirements and who will maintain the system.

sections.text: Will it work with your existing cameras?

For most organizations, replacing working cameras is not an option. Ask each vendor how they connect: through standards such as ONVIF and RTSP, through vendor SDKs, or only with their own cameras. Then ask for compatibility to be confirmed model by model against your actual list, including older cameras and recorders.

Ask, too, what camera conditions their detections need: resolution, angle, lighting, field of view and distance to the subject. A credible vendor will say which cameras are suitable as they are, which need adjusting and which are not suitable for a given detection. Our guide to [adding AI to existing CCTV cameras](/blogs/add-ai-to-existing-cctv-cameras) covers the compatibility checks, and the glossary entry on [video analytics](/glossary/video-analytics) explains the basics.
Where does AI inference run?
This one question shapes bandwidth, alert speed, privacy and resilience. Inference can run on a node at the site (the edge), in the vendor's cloud or in a mix of the two.
Ask:

items: Where exactly are frames analyzed, and on what hardware?
What hardware is needed at each site, and who sizes it?
How much upload bandwidth does each site need for analytics?
What keeps working when the internet link goes down: recording, detection, local alerts?

sections.text: Our [comparisons](/compare) set out the trade-offs, including on-premise versus cloud video analytics.
What data residency questions should you ask?
Even if your policies allow cloud processing, you need clear written answers about the data. Ask every vendor:

items: Does any video leave the site? If so, which video, when and why?
Where is video stored and processed, and in which country?
What metadata, snapshots or clips are sent to a central system?
Who at the vendor or its partners can access video, and is that access logged?
How long is each type of data retained, and how is it deleted?
Is customer video used to train or improve models?

sections.text: Involve IT security and legal early, and get the answers into the contract.
How does it manage many sites?

Look for one console across all sites, with role-based access so site staff, regional managers and auditors each see only their scope. Check how configuration, model updates and user changes are rolled out across sites, and whether a single alert queue covers every location. If you also need live view, recording and playback, check how the analytics relate to the [VMS](/solutions/vms).
Does it monitor camera health?

AI cannot detect anything on a camera that is offline, blocked, out of focus or not recording. Ask whether the platform monitors cameras, recorders, storage and network links, and whether it alerts on problems such as a camera that is online but has stopped recording, or one that has been tampered with. [Camera health monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring) is often what keeps analytics trustworthy after the first few months. If you will also track devices, warranties and maintenance, look at how [asset tracking](/solutions/asset-tracking) and [AMC management](/solutions/amc-management) connect to the same records.
How should you design a pilot?
A pilot is where claims meet reality. Design it so the result is clear whichever way it goes.

items: **Use your own cameras and sites**, including at least one difficult view, such as poor lighting or a busy scene.
**Agree success criteria in writing before it starts**: which events must be detected, how false alerts will be judged and how quickly operators must be able to act.
**Run it long enough to see normal variation**, including night, shift changes and weather.
**Involve the people who will use it**, not only the evaluation team.
**Record what happens:** missed events, false alerts and their causes, how easy rules were to tune, how operators felt about the alert volume and how the vendor responded when something went wrong.

sections.text: Treat the vendor's responsiveness during the pilot as a preview of support after purchase.
What integrations and support do you need?

Analytics are more useful when alerts reach the right people and systems. Ask how alerts are delivered and acknowledged, whether there is an API, and how the platform connects to existing VMS or NVRs, access control and ticketing tools. For support, ask who installs and maintains the system near your sites, how software updates are delivered and rolled back, and what happens when a site node or camera fails.
Finally, ask how pricing is structured, for example by cameras, sites, modules or support scope, so you can compare like with like. See how [OrionAlerts pricing](/pricing) works.
What should be on your evaluation checklist?
Use this table to score each vendor consistently, and agree the weighting with stakeholders before the first demo.

rows: Does it detect the events in your brief, at your sites?
Is compatibility confirmed model by model for your cameras and recorders?
Does it support ONVIF, RTSP and vendor SDKs, or only its own cameras?
Does inference run on site, in the cloud or both, and on what hardware?
Where is video stored and processed, and what leaves the site?
What keeps working during an internet outage?
Is there one console, alert queue and role model across sites?
Does it flag offline, tampered or non-recording cameras?
How are alerts delivered, acknowledged and escalated?
Is there an API, and does it work with your VMS, NVRs and other systems?
Did it meet the success criteria agreed in advance?
Who supports your sites, and how are updates rolled out and rolled back?

**Inference location and data residency:** in the standard deployment, video and AI processing stay on an on-site [Nebula OS](/nebula-os) node, with GPU acceleration where AI analytics are enabled. Only health status, alerts, configuration and operational metadata synchronize to Orion Cloud.
**Resilience:** recording and detection run on site, so they do not depend on a fast internet link.
**Multi-site management:** each site runs its own node, and Orion Cloud gives one view across locations, with role-based access for operators, managers and auditors.
**Camera health:** the Health Monitoring module flags cameras that are offline or have stopped recording, and asset tracking and AMC management share the same device records.
**Alert handling:** alerts reach the dashboard, mobile app and email, and zone and schedule rules decide which events raise an alert.

**Support model:** deployments can also be partner-managed, with system integrators and AMC providers running nodes for their clients.

sections.text: FAQs
How long should an AI video analytics pilot run?

Long enough to cover normal variation at the site, such as day and night, shift changes and busy and quiet periods. Agree the duration and success criteria with the vendor before the pilot starts, and extend it if a condition that matters, such as monsoon weather or a seasonal peak, has not yet occurred.
Do I need new cameras for AI video analytics?

Often not. Many platforms work with existing IP cameras through ONVIF, RTSP or vendor SDKs, and analog cameras can often be used through a DVR or encoder that provides a network stream. Some views may need repositioning or better lighting for specific detections, so a pilot should show which cameras are good enough before you buy new hardware.
Should AI video analytics run on site or in the cloud?

It depends on bandwidth, data policies, the number of cameras and how reliable your internet links are. On-site inference keeps video local and keeps working during outages; cloud inference needs less hardware at the site. Many multi-site organizations combine them, with inference at each site and management in one central console.
What is the most important thing to ask a vendor?

Ask to see the system working on your own cameras at your own sites, not on curated demo footage. A pilot with success criteria agreed in writing shows how detections cope with your lighting, angles and traffic, how noisy the alerts are and how the vendor responds when something needs fixing.

posts.title: How to Add AI to Existing CCTV Cameras Without Replacing Them
posts.seoTitle: How to Add AI to Existing CCTV Cameras
posts.excerpt: Add AI video analytics to the CCTV cameras you already own: compatibility checks, ONVIF and RTSP, edge vs cloud processing and a pilot-first rollout.
posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: Live analytics dashboard fed by existing site cameras, counting people and vehicles, checking helmets and vests, showing zone occupancy and listing alerts for an unauthorized person, a missing helmet and a vehicle in a restricted area
takeaways: Most IP cameras can feed AI analytics as they are, as long as their video stream can be reached over RTSP (usually located through ONVIF), directly or through the NVR.
Analog cameras usually need a DVR or encoder that exposes a network stream before AI can use them.
Run AI on an on-premise server or appliance when you want video to stay on site; check bandwidth before sending streams elsewhere.
Start with a pilot on a few cameras and use cases, tune zones and schedules, then scale the same policy across sites.
Replace cameras selectively, only where the view, resolution or device health cannot support the use case.

sections.text: **Short answer:** You can add AI to most existing CCTV cameras by sending their video streams to a separate AI server or appliance instead of replacing the cameras. IP cameras usually stream over RTSP, with ONVIF used for discovery and configuration, either directly or through the NVR; analog cameras need a DVR or encoder that provides a network stream. A short pilot then confirms which cameras and use cases work before you scale.

Most organizations already have more cameras than anyone can watch. The cameras are fine; what is missing is the ability to notice events while they are happening. Adding AI to the existing estate is usually faster and less disruptive than a rip-and-replace project, as long as you check a few things first.
Can you add AI to existing CCTV cameras?
Yes. In most cases AI video analytics run on a separate server that reads the video your cameras already produce, so the cameras themselves do not need to be "AI cameras".

[Video analytics](/glossary/video-analytics) software needs one thing from a camera: a usable video stream. Modern IP cameras provide this out of the box. The software decodes the stream, runs detection models on the frames and raises an alert when a rule is met, for example a person entering a restricted zone after hours.

That is different from cameras with built-in analytics, where detection runs on the camera's own chip. Built-in analytics can be useful, but they are tied to one camera model, are hard to manage consistently across brands and are limited by the camera's processing power. A central AI layer works across a mixed estate.
What should you check before adding AI?
Check the camera type, how its stream can be reached, the image quality at the point that matters and the network between the camera and the AI server.

items: **Camera type.** IP cameras are the easiest. Analog and HD-analog cameras record to a DVR and need the DVR or an encoder to provide a network stream.

**Stream access.** Confirm the camera or recorder supports [RTSP](/glossary/rtsp) and, ideally, [ONVIF](/glossary/onvif), and that you have the credentials. Many cameras offer a main stream and a lower-resolution substream.
**Image quality where it matters.** Ask whether the object you care about (a person, a helmet, a number plate) is large and sharp enough in the frame, day and night.
**Placement and lighting.** Backlight, glare, IR reflections and obstructions cause more problems than resolution alone.
**Network capacity.** Every stream sent to an AI server uses bandwidth. Check switch uplinks and any WAN links between sites.
**Recorder role.** Decide whether the existing NVR keeps recording, which is common, or whether recording moves to a new platform.

sections.text: How does the video reach the AI server?
There are three common paths, and many estates use more than one.
Directly from the camera

The AI server pulls the stream from each camera over RTSP, discovered and configured through ONVIF where supported. This gives the most direct, highest-quality feed and keeps the NVR out of the analytics path.
Through the NVR or DVR

Many recorders can re-stream the channels they record. This is useful when cameras sit on an isolated network behind the recorder, or when analog cameras are only reachable through a DVR. Check how many simultaneous streams the recorder can serve without affecting recording.
Through an encoder
For analog cameras without a suitable DVR, a video encoder converts the analog signal into an IP stream. It keeps working cameras in service while the analytics layer is added.
Where should the AI run: on site or in the cloud?
Run inference close to the cameras when you want raw video to stay on site and to avoid sending many streams over the internet; use a central layer for management, reporting and alert review.
**On the camera:** no extra hardware, but limited processing, vendor-specific features and uneven results across brands.

**On an on-premise server or appliance** ([edge AI](/glossary/edge-ai-video-analytics)): video stays inside the site network, latency is low and it works through weak or intermittent WAN links. You need hardware sized to the number of channels and use cases.
**In the cloud:** easy to start and centrally managed, but every analyzed stream must be uploaded, which can be costly or impractical at scale, and raw video leaves the site.

Many multi-site organizations combine on-site and central layers: an on-premise node at each site for video and inference, and a central console for alerts, health and configuration across all sites. Our guide to [edge vs cloud video analytics](/blogs/edge-vs-cloud-video-analytics) compares the options in more detail.
Which use cases work best on existing cameras?
Use cases that need a clear view of people or vehicles in a defined area usually work well on existing overview cameras; tasks that need fine detail may need a closer or dedicated camera.
Good first candidates:

items: [Perimeter intrusion detection](/use-cases/perimeter-intrusion-detection) and [restricted-zone monitoring](/use-cases/restricted-zone-monitoring)
[Loitering detection](/use-cases/loitering-detection) and [crowd detection](/use-cases/crowd-detection)
[Fire and smoke detection](/use-cases/fire-smoke-detection) as an additional early-warning layer
[Camera tampering detection](/use-cases/camera-tampering-detection) and [no-motion or black-screen alerts](/use-cases/no-motion-black-screen-alert)
[Vehicle detection](/use-cases/vehicle-detection) at gates and docks

sections.text: Use cases that often need better-placed cameras: [PPE detection](/glossary/ppe-detection), where the helmet or vest must be clearly visible, and [ANPR](/glossary/anpr), which depends on plate angle, shutter speed and lighting.
How do you roll it out step by step?
Treat the first deployment as a pilot that proves value on your own scenes, then scale the tuned policy.

items: **Inventory the estate.** List cameras, recorders, models, firmware and sites. An [asset register](/solutions/asset-tracking) helps here.
**Pick two or three use cases** with a clear owner and a clear response.
**Select pilot cameras** that represent your typical scenes, including night views.
**Draw zones and set schedules** so rules match how each area is actually used.
**Validate alerts in a pilot window.** Review every alert with the people who will respond, and tune thresholds.
**Define routing.** Decide who receives each alert type and how escalation works.
**Scale the policy** to more cameras and sites, and keep reviewing noisy rules.

sections.text: Monitor the health of the cameras you rely on from day one. An analytics rule on a camera that has gone offline fails silently; [camera health monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring) makes that visible.
When do you actually need new cameras?
Only where the existing view cannot support the use case: wrong position, too little detail, poor night performance or a failing device.

Replace selectively. A pilot will show which cameras produce reliable detections and which do not. Often the fix is to re-aim, refocus or clean a camera, add lighting, or add one dedicated camera for a demanding task such as ANPR, rather than replacing a whole estate.
How does OrionAlerts add AI to existing cameras?

OrionAlerts, built by Global Ace Technology Pvt. Ltd. in Mumbai, turns existing CCTV and IP cameras into real-time [AI video analytics](/solutions/ai-analytics) alerts without replacing the camera estate.

Its [Nebula OS](/nebula-os) device layer connects cameras through ONVIF, RTSP and vendor SDKs, so the estate stays brand-neutral. Nebula OS can run on an on-premise appliance or server next to the cameras, where video and AI inference stay inside the site network and only health, alerts and configuration metadata sync outward. Alerts reach teams through the dashboard, the mobile app and email, and the same platform includes a [VMS](/solutions/vms) and camera health monitoring. For a brand-specific example, see [CP Plus AI video analytics integration](/blogs/cp-plus-ai-video-analytics-integration).

For industry-specific examples, see the pages for [manufacturing](/industries/manufacturing), [logistics](/industries/logistics), [education campuses](/industries/education-campuses) and [commercial buildings](/industries/commercial-buildings).
FAQs
Do I need AI cameras to use AI video analytics?

No. Most AI video analytics run on a server or appliance that reads standard streams from ordinary IP cameras. Cameras with built-in analytics can help in individual spots, but a central AI layer applies the same detections and rules across a mixed estate of brands and models, which is easier to manage across many sites.
Can analog CCTV cameras be used for AI analytics?

Often, yes. Analog and HD-analog cameras need a DVR or video encoder that provides a network stream. Image quality then decides which use cases are realistic: older, lower-resolution cameras may handle intrusion or zone alerts well but struggle with detail-heavy tasks such as PPE checks or number-plate reading.
Will adding AI affect my existing NVR recording?

It should not, if planned well. Streams are usually pulled directly from the cameras, or from the NVR within its streaming capacity, while the NVR continues recording as before. Check that each camera can serve an extra stream, often its substream, and that the network has headroom for it.
How long does a pilot take?

It depends on the number of cameras, use cases and sites. Plan enough time to see day, night and shift-change conditions, and to tune zones and schedules at least once, before judging results. Agree the duration and the success criteria with the vendor in writing before the pilot starts.

posts.title: CCTV Camera Health Monitoring: Detect Offline Cameras and Recording Gaps Before an Incident
posts.seoTitle: CCTV Camera Health Monitoring: Detect Offline Cameras
posts.excerpt: How CCTV camera health monitoring finds offline cameras, blocked views and recording gaps before an incident, and what checks and metrics to use.
posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: Device status dashboard listing cameras, NVRs and servers across sites with online, warning and offline states, uptime and last-seen times
takeaways: A camera that answers a ping is not necessarily streaming or recording; health monitoring must check video and recording, not only the network.
Watch five layers: cameras, image quality, recording, storage and the network and servers behind them.
Route each fault to an owner, and to the right AMC vendor, so it becomes a tracked ticket rather than a forgotten email.
Measure camera availability, recording completeness and time to restore, site by site.

sections.text: **Short answer:** CCTV camera health monitoring continuously checks that every camera is online, delivering a usable picture and actually being recorded, and alerts the right person when any of that stops. It catches offline cameras, blocked or blurred views, full disks and recording gaps while they can still be fixed, instead of when footage is needed after an incident.

Most surveillance failures are not dramatic. A camera loses power after maintenance work. A disk fills up and the recorder stops writing. A camera is knocked out of position and now films a wall. Nobody notices until someone needs the footage, and by then the gap cannot be recovered.
What is CCTV camera health monitoring?
It is the continuous, automated checking of cameras, recorders, storage and network links, with alerts when any of them leaves a healthy state.

Manual "camera rounds", where someone clicks through every feed once a day or once a week, cannot keep up with large or multi-site estates. They also miss problems that do not show on a live view, such as a camera that streams fine but is not being recorded. [Camera health monitoring](/glossary/camera-health-monitoring) replaces those rounds with checks that run all the time and leave a record.
Why do camera failures go unnoticed?
Because most failures are silent: the video wall still shows a picture, the network still answers and nobody owns the question "is every camera recording right now?"
Common reasons:

items: **Network checks are not video checks.** A camera can answer a ping while its video stream has frozen or stopped.
**Live view hides recording problems.** An operator sees the live picture, not whether the recorder is writing it to disk.
**Image problems look like quiet scenes.** A camera turned toward a wall or covered in dust raises no error at all.
**Faults spread across systems.** Camera status is on one screen, recorder status on another and the disks somewhere else.
**No clear owner.** Security assumes IT is watching, IT assumes the AMC vendor is, and the vendor waits for a complaint.

sections.text: What should a health monitoring system check?
Check every layer between the lens and the stored file, because a failure at any one of them means lost evidence.

rows: Online status, stream availability, frame rate
Power loss, crashed cameras, frozen streams
Black screen, blur, obstruction, sudden scene change
Covered, moved, defocused or tampered cameras
Is each channel being written, and are there gaps?
Channels dropped from the schedule, recorder faults
Disk health, free capacity, retention days achieved
Failing disks, full volumes, retention below policy
Switch and link status, recorder and server services
Uplink failures, overloaded or offline recorders

sections.text: Image checks deserve special attention. [Camera tampering detection](/use-cases/camera-tampering-detection) and [no-motion or black-screen alerts](/use-cases/no-motion-black-screen-alert) find cameras that are technically online but useless. Our glossary explains [camera tampering detection](/glossary/camera-tampering-detection) in more detail.
Time synchronization is worth adding to the list. If recorders drift from the correct time, footage is harder to correlate across cameras and harder to rely on as evidence.
How do you catch recording gaps before an incident?
Compare what should be recorded with what actually was, every day, for every channel.

items: **Define the policy per camera:** continuous or event-based recording, and how many days must be retained.
**Check that each channel is writing** and flag any channel with no new footage within the expected window.
**Scan for gaps** in the stored timeline, not only for errors raised by the recorder.
**Track achieved retention** against the policy, so a site that keeps fewer days than required is flagged early.
**Alert on capacity trends**, not only on full disks, so storage is expanded before recording stops.

sections.text: Retention problems are especially easy to miss: everything appears to work, but the oldest footage is being overwritten sooner than the policy says.
How should health alerts be routed and fixed?
Every health alert needs an owner, a severity and a path to a fix; otherwise it becomes background noise like any other alarm.

items: **Severity by camera importance.** A perimeter or cash-office camera going offline is more urgent than a corridor camera.
**Owner by fault type.** Network faults go to IT, recorder and camera faults to the maintenance team or vendor.
**Tickets, not emails.** Raise a service request automatically, so every fault is tracked to closure.
**Contract context.** Show whether the device is under warranty or an [annual maintenance contract](/glossary/amc-annual-maintenance-contract), and which vendor is responsible.

sections.text: This is where health monitoring meets [AMC management](/solutions/amc-management). Our [CCTV AMC management checklist](/blogs/cctv-amc-management-checklist) covers SLAs, preventive maintenance and vendor scorecards.
Which metrics prove camera uptime?
Report a few metrics consistently, by site and by vendor, rather than a single estate-wide percentage.

items: **Camera availability:** the share of time each camera was online and streaming
**Recording completeness:** the share of required footage actually stored
**Retention compliance:** sites and channels meeting the retention policy
**Time to restore:** how long faults stay open, from detection to fix
**Repeat faults:** cameras or sites that fail again after being fixed

sections.text: These numbers turn uptime from an assumption into evidence, for internal audits, for leadership and for conversations with vendors.
How do you get started?
Start with an accurate register of devices, then add monitoring and routing in that order.

items: Build or clean up the list of cameras, recorders, disks and switches per site, ideally in an [asset register](/solutions/asset-tracking).
Agree recording and retention policies per camera group.
Turn on continuous checks for all layers, starting with your most critical sites.
Define owners and severity, and connect alerts to service tickets.
Review availability and repeat faults monthly with each vendor.

In OrionAlerts, [Health Monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring) is one of five modules on the same video intelligence platform.

It tracks the status of cameras, NVRs, servers, storage and network devices in real time, detects recording interruptions, storage capacity risk and retention issues, and provides uptime and availability reports. Health alerts reach the responsible team through the dashboard, the mobile app and email, and show whether the camera, NVR, storage or network is at fault. For multi-site estates, each site's node checks its own devices and Orion Cloud brings health status from every location into one view.

Because the health engine runs inside [Nebula OS](/nebula-os), it sees failures the network alone cannot, such as a camera that pings but has stopped recording. And because health, asset and AMC records share the same device, a camera fault can open a service request with the vendor whose contract covers that camera. The [VMS](/solutions/vms) and [AI video analytics](/solutions/ai-analytics) run on the same platform, so an alert from a camera and that camera's health status are never in separate systems.
FAQs
What is the difference between camera health monitoring and network monitoring?

Network monitoring checks whether a device is reachable. Camera health monitoring also checks whether the video stream works, whether the image is usable and whether the footage is being recorded and retained. The difference matters because a camera can answer a ping while its stream is frozen, its view is blocked or its recorder has stopped writing.
Can health monitoring detect a camera that has been moved or covered?

Yes, if it includes image checks as well as device checks. Tampering and scene-change detection flag cameras that are covered, defocused, moved or showing a black screen, and comparing each view with a saved reference image helps confirm what changed. Without image checks, a camera pointing at a wall still looks healthy.
How often should cameras be checked?

Continuously. Daily or weekly manual checks leave long windows in which a failure can go unnoticed, and they do not show whether footage is being recorded. Automated checks should run around the clock and alert on any change, while people review trends and repeat faults on a fixed schedule, such as monthly with each vendor.
Does camera health monitoring need new cameras?

No. It works with existing cameras and recorders by reading their status, streams and recordings, so it can be added to an estate that is already installed. The depth of checks can vary by device, so confirm which camera and recorder models report recording and storage status, not only whether they are online.

posts.title: CCTV AMC Management Checklist: SLAs, Preventive Maintenance and Vendor Scorecards
posts.seoTitle: CCTV AMC Management Checklist: SLAs & Scorecards
posts.excerpt: A practical CCTV AMC checklist: what the contract should cover, how to set SLAs, what preventive maintenance includes and how to score vendors.
posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: Maintenance history dashboard with service logs, technician and vendor records and spare parts used for CCTV equipment
takeaways: A CCTV AMC is only enforceable if it lists every covered device, defines priorities and states response and resolution targets for each.
Preventive maintenance should verify recording and retention, not only clean lenses and check cables.
Score vendors on SLA adherence, preventive maintenance completion, repeat faults and reporting quality, using ticket data rather than impressions.
Link the AMC to an asset register and camera health alerts so faults become tickets against the right contract automatically.

sections.text: **Short answer:** Managing a CCTV AMC (annual maintenance contract) well comes down to four things: a contract that lists every covered device with clear priorities and response and resolution targets, a preventive maintenance checklist that proves cameras are recording, tickets that track every fault to closure, and a vendor scorecard built from that ticket data. The checklist below covers each of them.

In India, organizations with a sizeable camera estate commonly rely on one or more vendors under an AMC to keep cameras, recorders and cabling working. The contract is signed once a year; the problems show up every day. Without a clear structure, it is hard to know whether the AMC is delivering what it promised.
What is a CCTV AMC?
A CCTV AMC is a yearly service contract in which a vendor maintains your surveillance equipment, usually covering preventive visits and repairs for a defined list of devices.

AMCs are commonly offered as **comprehensive**, where spare parts are included, or **non-comprehensive**, where the vendor provides labor and parts are billed separately. Which one makes sense depends on the age of the estate and how predictable you need maintenance spend to be. Our glossary entry on the [AMC (annual maintenance contract)](/glossary/amc-annual-maintenance-contract) covers the basics.
What should a CCTV AMC contract include?
Write the contract so that any dispute can be settled by looking at the asset list and the ticket history.

items: **Asset schedule:** every covered camera, recorder, disk, switch and power device, with serial number and location
**Coverage type:** comprehensive or non-comprehensive, and which parts or consumables are excluded
**Preventive maintenance:** frequency of visits and the checklist each visit must complete
**Priorities and SLAs:** response and resolution targets for each priority level
**Escalation matrix:** named contacts at both ends, and when each level is involved
**Spares and standby:** whether the vendor keeps critical spares or provides standby units
**Reporting:** what the vendor must report, how often and in what format
**Access and security:** rules for remote access, passwords and who can change configurations
**Remedies:** what happens when SLAs are missed, and the conditions for renewal or termination

sections.text: How should CCTV AMC SLAs be defined?
Define priorities by the impact of the fault, then agree response and resolution targets for each priority that fit your risk and your sites.

rows: Recorder down, a whole site not recording, perimeter cameras offline
Fastest response and resolution, on-site attendance, standby equipment
Several cameras offline in a sensitive area
Short response, resolution within the next working window
Single camera offline, degraded image or night performance
Response and resolution within scheduled working hours
Cosmetic issues, documentation, minor configuration changes
Handled at the next preventive visit

sections.text: Two details make SLAs enforceable. First, define when the clock starts: when the fault is detected or reported, not when the vendor acknowledges it. Second, measure response (someone is working on it) separately from resolution (the camera is recording again). Targets that are not measured from ticket timestamps are hard to enforce.
What belongs in a preventive maintenance checklist?
Each preventive visit should leave the estate verifiably recording, with evidence, not just cleaned.

items: Clean lenses, domes and housings, and remove obstructions such as cobwebs or foliage
Compare each view with a reference image to catch cameras that have shifted or lost focus
Check night performance, IR illumination and backlight compensation
Inspect mounts, cabling, connectors and weatherproofing
Check power supplies, PoE budgets and UPS backup
Check recorder health: disks, fans, temperature, error logs and free capacity
Verify that every channel is recording and that retention meets the policy
Confirm time synchronization on cameras and recorders
Apply approved firmware updates under change control
Review user accounts and default passwords
Record findings per device, with photos where useful, against the asset register

sections.text: How do you build a vendor scorecard?
Score vendors on outcomes you can measure from tickets and visit records, reviewed monthly and summarized for the renewal decision.

rows: Share of tickets responded to within target, by priority
Share of tickets resolved within target, by priority
Visits completed on schedule, with a full checklist
Devices that fail again soon after a fix
Camera availability and recording completeness for covered sites
Reports delivered on time, complete and accurate

sections.text: Keep the scorecard factual. Data from [SLA tracking](/solutions/amc-management) and [camera health monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring) is harder to argue with than a list of complaints.
How do you manage renewals and warranties?
Track every device's warranty and AMC coverage in one register, and get reminders well before anything expires.

New devices are often under manufacturer warranty when the AMC starts, so check for overlaps rather than paying twice. Devices that leave the estate should come off the asset schedule. And renewals should start early enough to use the scorecard in negotiations, rather than renewing automatically because time ran out. A live [asset register](/solutions/asset-tracking) with serial numbers, locations and documents makes all of this easier. Our guide to [building a live camera and NVR register](/blogs/surveillance-asset-management-register) covers what to record for each device.
What are the most common AMC mistakes?
Most AMC problems trace back to a vague contract or an untracked fault.

items: An asset list that is out of date on the day the contract is signed
Preventive visits that are signed off without verifying recording
Faults reported by phone or email with no ticket number or timestamp
One SLA for everything, so critical outages wait behind minor issues
No link between camera health alerts and the vendor who must fix them

sections.text: How does OrionAlerts help manage CCTV AMCs?
OrionAlerts includes [AMC Management](/solutions/amc-management) alongside Asset Tracking and Health Monitoring, so contracts sit on the same records as the devices they cover.

The module tracks AMC and warranty coverage against each asset and schedules preventive maintenance across sites. Service requests are logged from intake through vendor dispatch to closure. Vendors are measured on response time, completion quality and repeat issues against their SLAs, and at-risk tickets are flagged early. Reminders go out before AMC, warranty and contract renewals and preventive visits fall due.

Because [Nebula OS](/nebula-os) links health events to the contract already attached to each device, a camera that fails can generate a ticket for the responsible vendor automatically, instead of waiting for someone to notice and phone it in. Read [CCTV camera health monitoring](/blogs/cctv-camera-health-monitoring) for how faults are detected in the first place.
FAQs
What is the difference between a comprehensive and a non-comprehensive CCTV AMC?

A comprehensive AMC includes spare parts in the contract price, while a non-comprehensive AMC covers labor and visits and bills parts separately. Always check the exclusions list in either case: comprehensive contracts often still exclude physical damage, consumables or cabling, and non-comprehensive contracts should state how parts are quoted and approved.
How often should CCTV preventive maintenance be done?

It depends on the environment and the contract. Dusty, outdoor or industrial sites need more frequent visits than clean indoor sites. Agree a frequency per site type, write it into the contract and track completion, and use health data to bring a visit forward when a site shows repeat faults.
Who should own the AMC inside the organization?

One named owner, usually in facilities, administration or IT, should hold the contract, the scorecard and the renewal, with security and site teams raising and verifying tickets. That owner reviews the scorecard with the vendor every month and starts the renewal discussion well before the contract ends.
Can AMC management be automated?

Much of it can: asset and contract records, preventive maintenance schedules, ticket routing, SLA timers, reminders and scorecards. Site checks and repairs still need people. Automation works best when camera health alerts create tickets directly, so the SLA clock starts when a fault is detected rather than when someone reports it.

posts.title: VMS vs NVR: When Does a Multi-Site Enterprise Need a Video Management System?
posts.seoTitle: VMS vs NVR: When Do You Need a Video Management System?
