posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: Video management system architecture with IP cameras at an office, a factory and a warehouse connected over LAN or WAN to a central VMS core, storage and control-room, desktop, web and mobile clients
takeaways: An NVR is a recorder for a fixed set of cameras at one location; a VMS is software that manages cameras, recorders, users and events across many locations.
A single small site with one camera brand and a few users can run well on an NVR.
Multiple sites, mixed camera brands, a central control room, many users or audit needs are the usual signs you need a VMS.
You rarely have to rip out NVRs: a VMS can sit above them and take over central viewing, search and alarm handling in phases.

sections.text: **Short answer:** An NVR (network video recorder) records and plays back a fixed set of cameras at one location, while a VMS (video management system) is software that brings many cameras, recorders, users and sites into one console with alarms, search and access control. A multi-site enterprise usually needs a VMS once it has several locations, mixed camera brands, a central control room or audit requirements, and it can often keep its NVRs while adding one.

Most camera estates start with NVRs. A site gets cameras and a recorder, someone checks footage when needed, and it works. The trouble starts when there are ten, fifty or a hundred such sites, each with its own recorder, login and way of doing things.
What is the difference between an NVR and a VMS?
An NVR is a recording device; a VMS is a management platform. The NVR stores video for the cameras plugged into it, while the VMS manages video, users and events across the whole estate.

rows: A hardware recorder with built-in software
Software running on servers, appliances or the cloud
A fixed number of channels at one location
Best with the same brand; other brands vary
Multi-brand, usually through ONVIF, RTSP and vendor SDKs
Role-based access for many operators, managers and auditors
A shared queue with acknowledgment and escalation
Search across sites, with export and audit trails
Access control, analytics, ticketing and other systems

sections.text: The [glossary entry on NVR vs DVR vs VMS](/glossary/nvr-vs-dvr-vs-vms) adds the analog DVR to the comparison, and our [VMS](/glossary/vms) entry covers the term in more depth.
When is an NVR enough?
An NVR is enough when the estate is small, local and simple: one site, one camera brand, a handful of users and investigations done after the fact.

A single office, shop or small warehouse often fits this description. If nobody needs to watch several locations at once, footage is reviewed only occasionally and the person responsible sits on site, a good NVR is often the simplest and most economical answer.
When does a multi-site enterprise need a VMS?
When people need to see, search and act on video across locations from one place, with clear control over who can do what.
Typical signs:

items: **Several sites** that a central team must monitor or investigate across
**Mixed camera and recorder brands**, often from acquisitions or different installers
**A central or regional control room** that needs one live wall and one alarm queue
**Many users with different scopes**, such as site guards, regional managers and auditors
**Evidence and audit needs**, where exports and access must be logged
**Integrations** with access control, alarms or business systems
**Plans for AI analytics**, which work best on a managed, central video layer

sections.text: At that point, the cost of logging into dozens of recorders, chasing passwords and stitching together exports usually outweighs the cost of a VMS.
Do you have to replace your NVRs to move to a VMS?
Usually not. Many VMS platforms can connect to existing cameras and recorders, so NVRs can keep recording on site while the VMS handles central viewing, search and alarms.
A phased approach works well:

items: **Connect what exists.** Add existing cameras and recorders to the VMS, site by site.
**Centralize the workflow.** Move live monitoring, alarm handling and evidence export into the VMS console.
**Standardize policies.** Apply common roles, retention rules and naming across sites.
**Retire recorders on your schedule.** Replace NVRs when they reach end of life, not all at once.

sections.text: The same logic applies to cameras: keep the ones that work, and replace only where coverage or image quality is not good enough. Our guide on [adding AI to existing CCTV cameras](/blogs/add-ai-to-existing-cctv-cameras) covers the compatibility checks.
Where do AI analytics and camera health fit?
A VMS is the foundation; AI analytics and camera health monitoring are the layers that make a large estate manageable.

With [AI video analytics](/solutions/ai-analytics), the system flags events such as [perimeter intrusion](/use-cases/perimeter-intrusion-detection) or [unauthorized area entry](/use-cases/unauthorized-area-entry) instead of relying on operators to spot them. With [camera health monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring), the system shows which cameras are offline or not recording, which matters more as the number of sites grows. Both work best when they share the same device list and alarm queue as the VMS.

Some organizations prefer a cloud-hosted model, often called [VSaaS (video surveillance as a service)](/glossary/vsaas). Others keep video on site and use a central console for management. The right choice depends on bandwidth, data policies and how much video must leave each site.
How do you choose a VMS?
Choose on fit with your estate and workflow, and test it on your own cameras.

items: Does it support the camera and recorder brands you already own?
Can it show all sites in one console, with role-based access per site?
Does it have a shared alarm queue with acknowledgment, escalation and audit trails?
How fast can an investigator find and export footage across sites?
Does it work through limited or intermittent WAN links?
Can it add AI analytics and camera health monitoring without separate systems?
What does it need on site, and what runs centrally?

sections.text: How does OrionAlerts approach VMS?
OrionAlerts includes an enterprise [VMS](/solutions/vms) as one of the five modules of its video intelligence platform.

It provides centralized live monitoring and playback, multi-site management, video search and evidence export, secure remote access, event and alarm management from one shared queue, and open integration with IP cameras and third-party systems. Supported IP cameras and recorders connect through ONVIF, RTSP and vendor SDKs, so existing equipment is brought onto the platform rather than replaced.

The VMS runs on [Nebula OS](/nebula-os) together with AI video analytics, camera health monitoring, [asset tracking](/solutions/asset-tracking) and [AMC management](/solutions/amc-management). For multi-site estates, each site can run its own Nebula OS node for video, recording and inference, while Orion Cloud provides the central command view across every location. See how multi-site video management applies to industries such as [banking](/industries/banking), [retail](/industries/retail-shopping), [logistics](/industries/logistics) and [manufacturing](/industries/manufacturing).
FAQs
Is an NVR the same as a DVR?

No. A DVR records analog or HD-analog cameras, usually connected over coaxial cable, while an NVR records IP cameras over the network. A VMS can manage both, usually through the recorder or an encoder. Hybrid recorders that accept both analog and IP cameras are also common during migrations.
Can a VMS work with my existing NVRs?

Often, yes. Many VMS platforms connect to existing recorders and cameras, so you can centralize viewing and alarms first and replace recorders later. Check which recorder models and firmware versions are supported, whether playback and export work through the recorder, and how many streams each recorder can serve without affecting recording.
Do I need a VMS for a single site?

Not always. A single site with a few users and one camera brand can work well on an NVR. A VMS starts to pay off when there are many cameras, many users with different permissions, integrations with other systems, audit requirements or a control room that needs one alarm queue.
Is a VMS the same as video analytics?

No. A VMS manages, records and plays back video; video analytics detect events in it, such as an intrusion or a missing helmet. They can be bought separately, but platforms that combine the two let operators see an alert and the footage behind it in one place, without switching systems.

posts.title: AI PPE Detection for Factories: How It Works and How to Roll It Out
posts.seoTitle: AI PPE Detection for Factories: How It Works
posts.excerpt: How AI PPE detection works on factory CCTV, which PPE it can see reliably, what affects accuracy and a step-by-step rollout plan for plants.
posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: AI Vision dashboard flagging a missing helmet and missing gloves on factory workers, next to perimeter intrusion and unauthorized access alerts
takeaways: AI PPE detection finds people in a camera view, checks whether required items such as helmets and high-visibility vests are present and alerts when they are missing.
Large, distinctive items are easier to detect than small ones like gloves, goggles or ear protection, which need closer camera views.
Camera angle, distance, lighting, occlusion and look-alike clothing affect accuracy more than the model alone.
Roll out zone by zone with EHS: define the PPE required per zone, pilot, tune, route alerts to supervisors and track trends by shift.

sections.text: **Short answer:** AI PPE detection uses computer vision on CCTV streams to find each person in a defined zone, check whether the required protective equipment (such as a helmet or high-visibility vest) is visible and alert a supervisor when it is missing. It works on many existing factory cameras, but results depend on camera placement and on defining exactly which PPE each zone requires.

Every plant has PPE rules. The hard part is checking them consistently across every shift, entrance and production line. Supervisors cannot be everywhere, and spot checks only catch what happens while someone is looking. AI PPE detection gives EHS teams a continuous view of compliance, using cameras that are usually already installed.
What is AI PPE detection?
[PPE detection](/glossary/ppe-detection) is a video analytics use case that checks whether people in a camera view are wearing the personal protective equipment required in that area.

It is one form of [safety compliance detection](/use-cases/safety-compliance-detection). Instead of recording footage for later review, the system evaluates live video and raises an alert, with a snapshot or short clip, when a rule is broken. It is typically used at entrances to production areas, in hazardous zones, on loading docks and on construction sites.
How does AI PPE detection work?
It works in a short chain of steps, each of which can be tuned for your site.

items: **Ingest the stream.** The AI server reads the camera's video, usually over RTSP from the camera or recorder.
**Detect people.** A model finds each person in the frame.
**Check PPE.** A second step looks for the required items on or near each person, such as a helmet on the head or a vest on the torso.
**Apply the zone rule.** The check only counts inside the zone where that PPE is required, and only during the hours the rule applies.
**Confirm persistence.** Many systems require the violation to hold across several frames, which filters out momentary misses as people turn or pass behind machinery.
**Alert with evidence.** The system sends an alert with an image or clip to the responsible supervisor, who verifies and acts.

sections.text: Because the logic is "required PPE in this zone", not "PPE anywhere", the same camera can watch a walkway where helmets are optional and a production bay where they are mandatory.
Which PPE can AI detect reliably?
Large, distinctive items are the most reliable; small items need closer camera views and careful validation.

items: **Helmets and hard hats:** usually the best starting point, because they are visible from most angles
**High-visibility vests and jackets:** generally reliable, as long as other clothing is not similar in color
**Gloves, safety goggles, face shields, masks and ear protection:** possible, but they are small in the frame and often hidden by hands, tools or head angle
**Safety shoes:** difficult on typical overhead cameras, because feet are often out of view or occluded

sections.text: Validate every item on your own footage. Helmets and vests vary in color and style between plants, contractors and visitors, and the model should be checked against what your workers actually wear.
What affects PPE detection accuracy?
Most accuracy problems come from the scene, not the model, so camera placement and zone design matter as much as the software.

items: **Distance and size in frame:** the further away a person is, the fewer pixels describe their helmet or gloves
**Camera angle:** steep overhead views hide faces and torsos; very low views are blocked by people and equipment
**Lighting:** backlight from doorways, glare, low light and IR night images all reduce detail
**Occlusion:** machinery, racks, vehicles and other workers can hide the PPE being checked
**Look-alike clothing:** brightly colored uniforms or caps can be mistaken for vests or helmets
**Environment:** dust, steam, smoke, rain and dirty lenses blur the image
**Crowding:** dense groups at shift change make it harder to associate PPE with the right person

sections.text: Treat accuracy as something you measure during a pilot on your own cameras, rather than a number on a datasheet.
Where should PPE rules apply in a factory?
Apply rules where the requirement is clear and the camera view is good, starting with the highest-risk areas.

Good first zones include the entrances to production halls, where everyone passes and can be checked consistently; hazardous areas such as furnaces, chemical stores, presses and high-voltage rooms; loading docks and yards with vehicle movement; and maintenance or construction areas within the plant. Combine PPE checks with [restricted-zone monitoring](/use-cases/restricted-zone-monitoring) where only trained staff should enter, and with [fall detection](/use-cases/fall-detection) or [fire and smoke detection](/use-cases/fire-smoke-detection) where those risks exist.
How do you roll out AI PPE detection?
Plan it with EHS and production, pilot it on a few zones and scale only once alerts are trusted.

items: **Define a PPE matrix.** For each zone, list the required PPE, the hours and any exemptions, such as escorted visitors.
**Survey cameras.** Check which existing cameras see each zone clearly; add or re-aim cameras only where needed. See [how to add AI to existing CCTV cameras](/blogs/add-ai-to-existing-cctv-cameras).
**Pilot two or three zones.** Include day and night shifts and shift changes.
**Tune rules.** Adjust zones, persistence and schedules with the supervisors who will receive alerts.
**Set routing.** Send alerts to the zone's supervisor first, with escalation to EHS for repeated or serious cases.

**Communicate with the workforce.** Explain what is monitored, why and how alerts are used, ideally as a coaching tool rather than only for discipline. Involve HR and your legal team on privacy questions.
**Scale and review.** Extend the tuned policy to more zones and sites, and review trends monthly.

sections.text: How do you measure success?
Look at trends and responses, not at a single compliance figure.

items: Compliance trend by zone, shift and contractor
Locations and times with repeated violations
Share of alerts verified as genuine by supervisors
Time from alert to supervisor response
Changes after training, signage or layout improvements

sections.text: How does OrionAlerts handle PPE detection?

OrionAlerts supports PPE and safety compliance detection as part of its [AI video analytics](/solutions/ai-analytics), alongside intrusion, restricted-area entry, line crossing, crowd and occupancy, vehicle detection, fire and smoke, loitering and process compliance.

It checks for required PPE, such as hard hats and high-visibility vests, in designated zones and shifts on existing IP cameras connected through ONVIF, RTSP and vendor SDKs. Zone and schedule rules keep alerts in line with how each area operates, violations reach supervisors on the dashboard, the mobile app and email, and each event is kept for safety reviews and audits. In [manufacturing](/industries/manufacturing), the same cameras can also watch restricted areas, machine zones and process workflows. The same approach applies in [cement](/industries/cement), [metals and mining](/industries/metals-mining), [pharma](/industries/pharma), [construction](/industries/construction) and [oil and gas](/industries/oil-gas). Keeping cameras working matters too; see [CCTV camera health monitoring](/blogs/cctv-camera-health-monitoring).
FAQs
Can AI PPE detection use our existing factory cameras?

Often, yes. Existing IP cameras can be used if their streams are accessible and they show the zone clearly enough. Analog cameras need a DVR or encoder that provides a network stream. A camera survey and pilot show which views work and where a camera should be re-aimed or added.
Does PPE detection identify individual workers?

PPE detection checks whether required equipment is present on a person in a zone; it does not need to identify who the person is. Any link to identity should be a separate, deliberate policy decision, agreed with HR and legal teams and explained to the workforce before rollout.
Which PPE should we start with?

Start with items that are both mandatory and clearly visible on your cameras, usually helmets and high-visibility vests, then add smaller items once those alerts are trusted. Production-hall entrances make a good first zone, because everyone passes at a similar distance from the camera and results are easy to judge.
What happens when the system raises a PPE alert?

The responsible supervisor receives the alert with an image or clip, verifies it and takes the agreed action, such as stopping work until PPE is worn. The response is recorded so trends can be reviewed later. Repeated alerts in the same zone or shift usually point to a training, supply or layout problem rather than to one person's behavior.

posts.author: OrionAlerts Team
posts.imageAlt: OrionAlerts alarm console with a live alarm feed tagged by severity, event details with assign and escalate controls, and alarm trends over 24 hours
takeaways: Alert fatigue happens when operators receive more alerts than they can meaningfully assess, so they start ignoring or bulk-clearing them.
Most noise comes from system design: generic rules, poor camera placement, no schedules, no routing and unmonitored camera faults.
Fix it by tuning rules per camera and zone, prioritizing by severity, routing to the right role and keeping cameras healthy.
Track acknowledgment time, the share of alerts that lead to action and repeat noise sources to prove it is improving.

sections.text: **Short answer:** Alert fatigue in CCTV control rooms is what happens when operators get more alarms than they can meaningfully assess, so real incidents get missed among false ones. It is fixed with better system design (tuned detection zones and schedules, severity-based prioritization, role-based routing and healthy cameras), not by asking people to try harder.

Security operations teams rarely struggle because they lack cameras. They struggle because the alerts that matter are lost in the volume. When every motion event competes for attention, true exceptions are noticed late, or not at all.
What is alert fatigue in video surveillance?
Alert fatigue is the gradual loss of attention that sets in when most of the alerts a team receives turn out to need no action.

The pattern is familiar to anyone who has worked a control-room shift. A new analytics rule goes live, the alert queue fills up, operators open the first few events carefully, and then they start skimming. Within weeks, alerts are acknowledged in batches, sounds are muted and some rules are quietly switched off. The cameras are still there and the software is still running, but nobody is really listening to it anymore.

It is the same problem hospitals and IT operations teams describe with monitoring alarms: when the ratio of meaningful alerts to noise drops, people adapt by tuning out. In video surveillance it is made worse by scale. A site with hundreds of cameras can generate a steady stream of motion and analytics events every hour.
Why do more alerts make sites less safe?
Because unfiltered detections create a false sense of coverage: the dashboard looks busy, but the one alert that matters is buried among the ones that do not.

items: Low-confidence events crowd out critical exceptions
Missing context forces operators to open multiple feeds manually
No role-based routing means everyone sees everything, so no one owns anything
Camera downtime adds silent gaps that look like quiet sites

sections.text: The costs are real even when they are hard to put a number on. Response to genuine incidents slows down. Night shifts inherit noisy policies they did not design. Investigations take longer because the event history is full of junk. And the investment in analytics stops paying back, because a system people ignore protects nothing.
What causes false alarms in CCTV analytics?
Most false alarms come from rules that do not match the scene, not from the detection model alone.
Common causes include:

items: **Generic rules applied everywhere.** Simple motion detection fires on headlights, rain, shadows, trees, insects near the lens and moving machinery.
**Wrong camera for the job.** A wide overview camera cannot reliably confirm a hard hat at the far end of a shop floor; a camera facing the sun at dusk will struggle every evening.
**No schedules.** A person in a loading bay is normal at 3 pm and suspicious at 3 am. Rules that ignore shift patterns alert on routine work.
**Zones drawn too large.** A restricted-area rule that includes a public footpath will alert on every passer-by.
**Duplicate coverage.** Several cameras watching the same gate each raise their own alert for one event.
**Unhealthy cameras.** Blurred, shifted or flickering views produce erratic detections, while offline cameras produce none at all.

sections.text: How does AI prioritization reduce false alarms?

AI video analytics reduce noise by detecting specific objects and behaviors (a person, a vehicle, missing PPE, smoke) instead of any pixel change, while rules attach a severity and an owner to each event.

The difference between a motion alarm and an analytics event is context. A motion alarm says "something changed". A well-configured [video analytics](/glossary/video-analytics) rule says "a person entered the chemical store outside working hours" and attaches a snapshot or short clip so the operator can verify it in seconds.
Prioritization then decides what reaches a human first:

items: **Severity.** [Fire and smoke](/use-cases/fire-smoke-detection) or a [perimeter breach](/use-cases/perimeter-intrusion-detection) outranks a vehicle parked too long.
**Confidence and persistence.** Requiring a detection to hold across several frames filters out one-frame glitches.
**Zone and schedule.** The same detection can be critical in one zone and irrelevant in another.
**Ownership.** Safety events go to EHS, perimeter events to security, camera faults to maintenance.

sections.text: In OrionAlerts, [AI video analytics](/solutions/ai-analytics) run with zone and schedule rules so alerts match how the site actually operates, and events reach people through the dashboard, the mobile app and email. Operators work from one shared queue in the [VMS](/solutions/vms), where they can acknowledge, escalate and clear incidents with clear ownership.
How do you fix alert fatigue step by step?
Treat it as an operations project: measure the noise, tune the worst sources, route the rest and keep the camera estate healthy.

items: **Audit the queue.** Export a few weeks of alerts and group them by camera, rule and hour. A small number of cameras and rules usually produce most of the noise.
**Retire or rewrite the worst rules.** Replace generic motion alarms with specific detections, tighten zones and add schedules.
**Fix the cameras behind the noise.** Re-aim, refocus, clean or relocate cameras that cause repeated false alerts.
**Define severity and ownership.** Agree which events are critical, who owns each type and what the expected response is.
**Pilot before scaling.** Validate new rules on a few cameras in a pilot window, then roll the same policy out across sites.

**Monitor camera health.** Use [camera health monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring) so offline cameras and recording gaps are visible, and handle [tampering](/use-cases/camera-tampering-detection) as its own alert type.
**Review monthly.** Treat noisy rules like defects: log them, fix them and check that they stay fixed.

sections.text: Searchable video for after-action review and estate health monitoring complete the picture, so operators are not fighting noisy alerts and broken cameras at the same time. Together, they let multi-site teams stay responsive as the camera estate grows.
Which metrics show it's improving?
Track whether alerts are acted on, how fast and where the noise comes from, rather than only how many alerts the system produces.

items: **Alerts per operator per shift**, trending down without losing genuine incidents
**Actionable rate:** the share of alerts that lead to a response, investigation or ticket
**Time to acknowledge** for critical alerts, by shift and site
**Top noise sources:** the cameras and rules that generate the most dismissed alerts
**Camera availability:** how many cameras were online and recording during the period

sections.text: Set your own baseline before you change anything, then compare month to month. The goal is not more detections; it is fewer interruptions, each one worth acting on.
FAQs
Is alert fatigue the same as false alarms?

No. False alarms are one cause. Alert fatigue can also come from true but low-value alerts, duplicate alerts for the same event and alerts sent to people who cannot act on them. Reducing false alarms helps, but severity levels, routing and duplicate suppression matter just as much.
Will adding AI analytics automatically reduce alert fatigue?

Not automatically. AI detections are more specific than motion alarms, but they still need sensible zones, schedules, severity levels and routing, plus cameras that are positioned and maintained for the job. A pilot that reviews every alert with the people who will respond is the quickest way to find the noisy rules.
Where should a multi-site team start?

Start with the sites and rules that generate the most dismissed alerts, fix those first and reuse the tuned policy elsewhere. Our guide to [VMS vs NVR](/blogs/vms-vs-nvr) covers how a central console helps, and [adding AI to existing CCTV cameras](/blogs/add-ai-to-existing-cctv-cameras) covers the rollout.

Unlike an NVR, which records, or a VMS, which views and manages video, it is built to drive decisions.

Many buyers still evaluate video as a device purchase: how many cameras, what resolution, how many days of storage. A vision intelligence platform reframes the question: how do we convert continuous visual data into prioritized actions for security, safety and operations teams?
What does a vision intelligence platform do?
It watches video so people do not have to, and hands them only the moments that need a decision, with the evidence attached.
In practice that means four jobs running together:

items: **Detect:** apply AI models to live streams to recognize people, vehicles, PPE, smoke, crowding or entry into restricted zones.

How is it different from an NVR, a VMS or video analytics?

Each layer answers a different question: an NVR asks "is it recorded?", a VMS asks "can we see and find it?", analytics ask "did something happen?" and a platform asks "who needs to act, and is the system able to see it at all?"

rows: Record and play back cameras on one recorder
View, manage and search video across recorders and sites
Turn video events into prioritized, owned actions
Routed alerts, evidence, reports and maintenance tickets
Monitored as part of the system

sections.text: The terms overlap in marketing, so it helps to read our glossary entries on [NVR vs DVR vs VMS](/glossary/nvr-vs-dvr-vs-vms), [VMS](/glossary/vms) and [video analytics](/glossary/video-analytics). For a deeper look at the first two layers, see [VMS vs NVR: when does a multi-site enterprise need a VMS?](/blogs/vms-vs-nvr)
What are the core components?
A complete platform combines six building blocks that share the same device and event records.
Device connectivity

A device layer that connects cameras and recorders from different brands, typically through [ONVIF](/glossary/onvif), [RTSP](/glossary/rtsp) and vendor SDKs, so the estate is not locked to one manufacturer.
Video management
Live view, recording, playback, search and evidence export, with role-based access. This is the classic [VMS](/solutions/vms) layer.
AI video analytics
Detection models and a rules engine that run on live streams, on site or in the cloud. [Edge AI video analytics](/glossary/edge-ai-video-analytics) keep inference close to the cameras.
Alert and incident workflow
Severity, routing, acknowledgment, escalation and an audit trail, so every alert has an owner and an outcome.
Camera health monitoring

Continuous checks on cameras, recorders, storage and network links, so offline cameras and recording gaps are found before an incident. See [camera health monitoring](/glossary/camera-health-monitoring).
Asset and maintenance records
A register of every device, with warranty, AMC coverage, service history and vendor SLAs, so a fault becomes a ticket against the right contract.
Why do deployments start with security and expand to operations?
Many deployments begin with security outcomes, but the same cameras can then support safety and operations, because they already point at the places where work happens.

Typical first projects are perimeter awareness, after-hours intrusion and restricted zones. Once those are working, teams add [PPE and safety compliance](/use-cases/safety-compliance-detection) on production floors, vehicle and dock activity in [logistics](/industries/logistics), crowding on campuses and process monitoring in regulated environments such as [pharma](/industries/pharma). The platform does not change; the rules and the owners of each alert do.
How do you evaluate a vision intelligence platform?
Judge it on workflow fit, from alert to investigation to maintenance, rather than on the length of the detection list.
Use this checklist when comparing vendors:

items: **Existing cameras.** Does it work with the cameras and recorders you already own, and how is compatibility checked model by model?
**Where video is processed.** Can inference run on site, so raw video stays inside your network, with only alerts and metadata sent to a central console?
**Noise control.** Can you set zones, schedules, severity and persistence per camera, and pilot rules before rolling them out?
**Routing and ownership.** Can alerts go to different teams by type and site, with acknowledgment and escalation recorded?
**Multi-site policy.** Can one tuned policy be applied across many sites, while site teams see only their own scope?
**Camera health.** Will it tell you when a camera is offline, obstructed or not recording, not only when it detects an event?
**Assets and AMC.** Are devices, warranties, AMC contracts and service tickets connected to the same records as the alerts?
**Evidence.** How quickly can an investigator find, review and export the clip behind an alert?
**Integration.** Are there APIs to connect access control, ticketing or ERP systems?
**Pilot terms.** Will the vendor validate the use cases on your own cameras and scenes before you commit?

sections.text: Ask every vendor to demonstrate these on footage from your own site. A demo on curated sample video says little about how a model will behave with your lighting, angles and traffic. Our [AI video analytics buyer's guide](/blogs/ai-video-analytics-buyers-guide) adds a full evaluation checklist and pilot plan.
Where does OrionAlerts fit?

OrionAlerts is an enterprise video intelligence platform of this kind, from Global Ace Technology Pvt. Ltd., Mumbai, India. It turns existing CCTV and IP cameras into real-time AI video analytics alerts, and combines a VMS, camera health monitoring, asset tracking and AMC management on Nebula OS, its Linux-based operating system.

The modules are [AI video analytics](/solutions/ai-analytics) for detection, the [VMS](/solutions/vms) for live view, playback and investigation, [health monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring) for camera and recording status, and [asset tracking](/solutions/asset-tracking) and [AMC management](/solutions/amc-management) so uptime stays part of the operating model. Because they run on [Nebula OS](/nebula-os) with one device model, a detection, a camera outage, an asset record and a maintenance ticket all refer to the same device. If you are starting from an existing estate, read [how to add AI to existing CCTV cameras](/blogs/add-ai-to-existing-cctv-cameras).
FAQs
Is a vision intelligence platform the same as a VMS?

No. A VMS manages, views and records video. A vision intelligence platform includes those functions and adds AI detection, alert workflows, camera health monitoring and asset and maintenance records on the same device records. The aim is for video to drive decisions and maintenance actions, not only to be stored and reviewed.
Do I need new cameras to use one?

Usually not. Most platforms work with existing IP cameras that provide standard streams, but compatibility should be checked model by model, and some scenes may need a better-positioned camera. Analog cameras usually need a DVR or encoder that provides a network stream before analytics can use them.
Is it only for security teams?

No. Security is the usual starting point, but safety, operations, facilities and maintenance teams can use the same platform for PPE compliance, occupancy, process exceptions and camera uptime. Each team sees the alerts and sites in its own scope, while the cameras, rules and device records stay shared.

sections.text: **Short answer:** Traditional CCTV monitoring depends on someone watching the right screen at the right second, which stops working once a site has more feeds than operators. AI video analytics keep the existing cameras but add an intelligence layer that detects defined events and alerts the right person in real time, so the footage is used to act, not only to investigate.

For years, enterprise security teams treated CCTV as a recording system: install cameras, store footage, review clips after something goes wrong. That model still has value for investigations, but it no longer matches how modern plants, campuses and logistics sites actually operate.
What does passive CCTV monitoring really cost?
The hidden cost is the gap between what the cameras see and what anyone acts on in time.

As camera estates grow, that gap widens. A site may have hundreds of feeds, yet only a handful of operators. Many events are missed in real time, then reconstructed later under pressure. The result is slow response, incomplete context and [alert fatigue](/blogs/alert-fatigue-is-an-ops-problem).

items: Manual monitoring cannot watch every zone continuously

sections.text: More cameras without better triage do not make operations safer; they create more footage to ignore.
How does AI video analytics change CCTV monitoring?
It moves the job from watching video to responding to alerts: the system evaluates every stream continuously and surfaces only the events that match a policy.

Instead of asking operators to stare at walls of video, [AI video analytics](/solutions/ai-analytics) evaluate streams for [intrusion](/use-cases/perimeter-intrusion-detection), PPE exceptions, [crowding](/use-cases/crowd-detection), [restricted-zone entry](/use-cases/restricted-zone-monitoring) and other policy events, then route high-confidence alerts with evidence attached.

That shift is what turns CCTV from a passive archive into an operational sensor network. Existing cameras stay in place; see [how to add AI to existing CCTV cameras](/blogs/add-ai-to-existing-cctv-cameras). The upgrade is the intelligence layer on top: prioritized alerts, searchable video and multi-site command through a [VMS](/solutions/vms).
What does good look like for enterprise teams?
High-performing teams do not eliminate human judgment. They protect it with fewer, better signals, faster investigations and cameras that are known to be working.

They shorten investigation cycles with searchable video and evidence export, and they keep camera estates healthy with [camera health monitoring](/solutions/health-monitoring) so blind spots do not appear silently overnight.

If your current model depends on someone noticing the right feed at the right second, it is already behind the operational reality of modern facilities. The next standard is simple: detect early, notify the right role and investigate with evidence that is already organized.
FAQs
Do we need new cameras to move beyond passive monitoring?

Usually not. AI video analytics can run on supported existing IP cameras, so the upgrade is the analytics layer rather than the cameras. Compatibility should be checked model by model, and a pilot shows which views are good enough for each use case. See [how to add AI to existing CCTV cameras](/blogs/add-ai-to-existing-cctv-cameras).
Does AI video analytics replace control-room operators?

No. It changes their job from watching screens to deciding what to do about specific events. Operators still verify alerts, judge context and coordinate the response; the system makes sure the right events reach them with evidence attached, and that cameras that stop working do not go unnoticed.
